digest.intro: Deep time, infrastructure war, and the physics you can finally see.

items.title: Iran's shadow move: tankers loitering over subsea cables
items.blurb: Three sanctioned Iranian tankers and a fishing boat have been tracked by maritime intelligence firm Windward slowly circling — then going dark, AIS off — directly over six active cables in the Strait of Hormuz. Those cables carry a third of India's westbound internet traffic and are the sole external connection for Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar. This is what infrastructure warfare looks like before the first cut.

items.title: The Bantu expansion: ancient DNA finally traces the mechanics
items.blurb: New ancient DNA work is tracing how Bantu-speaking peoples spread language, genes, and material culture together across sub-Saharan Africa over millennia — one of history's largest cultural migrations, now legible at the molecular level. The Great Zimbabwe ironworks are a touchstone: natural-draft furnaces wide enough to span an adult's arm, smelting at 2,100°F without bellows, producing industrial-scale iron across a network that stretched a continent. The story of how a culture propagates — what it carries, what it loses — turns out to be readable in both pottery clay and chromosomes.

items.title: A billion years of missing rock — solved
items.blurb: The Great Unconformity is geology's strangest wound: across multiple continents, you can touch rock from two eras separated by up to a billion years with no layers in between — a quarter of Earth's history simply absent. New research published in Nature fingers mantle dynamics: deep processes lifted continents above sea level, where ice sheets then ground them flat. The Cambrian explosion of complex life appears right at the younger edge of that gap, which may not be a coincidence.

items.title: Why astrophysics needs to stop chasing the Big Questions
items.blurb: In astrophysics, 'nuisance' is a quasi-technical term for anything that obscures the signal you're hunting — dust, ionized gas, ordinary matter itself. This essay argues that the field's hierarchy of prestige (dark matter, the multiverse, origins) has quietly inverted the actual epistemics: the 'nuisances' are often where the real science lives. It's a sharp critique of how mythology colonizes method, dressed as a cosmology essay.

items.title: Bambu Lab H3C: nine-tool changer comes to desktop
items.blurb: Bambu just announced the H3C, a desktop machine with a motorized nine-tool magazine that physically lowers toward the build area — nine separate Bowden tools, color-coded, swapping without the long purge paths that waste material in AMS-style systems. The practical upshot: multi-material prints that are faster, cleaner, and dramatically less wasteful on the bench. The technical details are still thin, but the form factor puts tool-changer capability at a price point the field hasn't seen.

items.title: An animated film made in Excel
items.blurb: Maria Tomazou made a full animated film inside Excel — not as a stunt, but as a genuine meditation on the pointless impulse to make things. The constraint isn't the joke; it's the whole argument: that the medium's absurdity is exactly what gives the act its integrity. She's also the person behind a remarkable stop-motion piece, which makes this a consistent practice, not a one-off.

items.title: Arkivism: 4 million public domain images, searchable by description
items.blurb: Arkivism indexes 4 million+ images from dozens of museums and archives — photos, illustrations, video, artworks — and lets you search them with a plain-language description the way you'd query a chatbot. The creator's explicit framing is 'antidote to generative AI': human-made results, no training data extraction, just discovery. Practically useful for visual research; philosophically pointed at this exact moment.

items.title: We attribute personalities to chatbots even when we know better
items.blurb: Research from Johannes Gutenberg University found that people not only anthropomorphize chatbots — they do it even after correctly identifying the text as AI-generated. The 'ELIZA effect,' named for Weizenbaum's 1960s chatbot whose users immediately began confiding in it, turns out to be robust to explicit knowledge; knowing doesn't immunize you. For anyone designing interfaces or interactive work, this is less a warning than a material property.

items.title: Superfluid helium: seeing quantum physics with your own eyes
items.blurb: Veritasium gets access to superfluid helium — the world's coldest liquid — and films quantum phenomena that are normally invisible: vortices, zero-viscosity flow, the stuff that only exists at temperatures near absolute zero made suddenly, shockingly visible. Derek Muller is reliable at exactly this: turning the abstract into something you can watch happen. Worth the 20 minutes.

facts.fact: Four countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar — have zero internet connections to the outside world except through undersea cables running through the Strait of Hormuz, the same chokepoint where Iranian-linked ships are now loitering.

The natural-draft iron-smelting furnaces near Great Zimbabwe were so efficiently designed that they sucked in air through a chimney without any human labor — no bellows required — at temperatures exceeding 2,100°F.

The Great Unconformity represents up to a quarter of Earth's total history simply missing from the rock record — in places like the Grand Canyon, you can touch layers 540 million and 2 billion years old with nothing in between.
In astrophysics, 'ordinary matter' — everything we can see and touch — is officially classified as a 'nuisance' by researchers studying dark matter via weak gravitational lensing.

Joseph Weizenbaum noticed in the 1960s that users of ELIZA — the world's first chatbot, a simple pattern-matching program — immediately began sharing deeply personal secrets with it, before the word 'chatbot' even existed.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film-essay that treats memory, ritual, and technology as systems — moving between Tokyo and Guinea with a camera that thinks. The invisible architecture of how cultures encode meaning is everywhere; nothing is decorative.

art_picks.title: I Am Sitting in a Room
art_picks.creator: Alvin Lucier
art_picks.why: One man, one room, one sentence recorded and played back until the room's resonant frequencies eat the words entirely — pure systems art that turns acoustics into something hallucinatory and inevitable. Obsessive depth, beautiful surface.

art_picks.title: The Paintings for the Temple
art_picks.creator: Hilma af Klint
art_picks.why: Abstract systems built from spiritualism, biology, and geometry decades before the word 'abstract art' existed — she kept them hidden for 20 years because she believed the world wasn't ready. The gap between the work's internal rigor and its cosmic ambition is exactly the kind of unreasonable depth that hooks you.

events.name: Tom Thayer: A Biography of the Sun
events.why: Thayer makes mythological theater from handmade materials — puppet cosmologies, solar cycles, folk-art fabrication — a one-person system for reimagining what images are for; opening day is today.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 West 53rd Street
events.why: Freestanding screens in MoMA's outdoor garden play hallucinatory images generated from fMRI brain scans and visitor gaze data in real time — a living question about whether machine vision can reconstruct thought; last few weeks.

events.name: Cristina Iglesias: Possible Matter
events.why: An immersive dome installation alongside wall sculptures that dissolve the boundary between built and natural environments — the kind of spatial work that makes you rethink how architecture and ecology share a nervous system.

events.name: Art Week NYC (inaugural)
events.venue: Citywide — Chelsea, Tribeca, LES, UES, New Museum (Midtown hub)
events.why: 76+ galleries opening simultaneously with editor-led walks and artist talks — worth it not for the brand but for the density: four days where every serious gallery in New York is showing something new at once.

events.name: Per Kirkeby: Shadows to the Feast
events.why: Kirkeby sat at the exact intersection of geology, abstraction, and poetry — a painter who understood deep time as a painterly problem; this opens during Art Week, so easy to combine.
